title: How to Check a Screen for Dead Pixels
description: Run a careful dead pixel check in five minutes, then work out whether the mark is a pixel, dust, or panel damage.
html:
A dead pixel check is simple: show one clean color at a time and look for a point that refuses to match. The trick is removing the usual distractions first.

Before you start

Wipe the screen with a clean microfiber cloth. A tiny spot of dust can look exactly like a failed pixel on a bright background.

Let the display warm up for 10 minutes. Use its native resolution, turn off any blue light filter, and set brightness to a comfortable level. You do not need to push it to 100 percent.

Run the color test

Open the dead pixel test and enter fullscreen. Check these colors in order:

  1. Black
  2. White
  3. Red
  4. Green
  5. Blue

Stand at your normal viewing distance first. Then move closer and scan the panel in a slow grid. Give extra attention to the corners and the area around the taskbar, since marks there are easy to miss during normal use.

Read what you see

A point that stays black on every bright color may be a dead pixel. A point that stays red, green, or blue may be a stuck subpixel. A dark smudge that changes shape when you move your head is more likely to be dust, pressure damage, or something behind the panel surface.

Take a photo on two different test colors. Focus the camera on the pixel grid, not on your reflection. The pair of photos gives a retailer or manufacturer much better evidence than one blurry shot.

Do not press the panel

Pixel massage advice is common and risky. Pressing a modern LCD or OLED panel can spread pressure damage, scratch the coating, or create a larger bright patch. Use the warranty route first.

What to do next

Check the seller's return window and the maker's pixel policy. Policies vary by panel type, pixel location, and the number of affected pixels. If the display is new, report the issue before the return period ends.

Repeat the test once after reconnecting the display cable or restarting the device. If the same point remains in the same physical place on every input, the panel is the likely cause.

title: How to Check Backlight Bleed Without Fooling Yourself
description: Test an LCD for edge glow in a realistic room and separate backlight bleed from IPS glow and camera exaggeration.
html:
Backlight bleed appears as bright patches near the edge of an LCD when the screen should look black. It is easiest to see at night, which is also when people accidentally make the test far harsher than normal use.

Set up a fair test

Use the room lighting you normally have while watching a dark film or playing a dark game. A completely black room with the display at maximum brightness can make a healthy panel look terrible.

Set brightness between 30 and 50 percent. Turn off local dimming for the first pass so it does not hide the panel's baseline behavior. Sit directly in front of the display at your usual distance.

Show a black screen

Open the dead pixel test, choose black, and enter fullscreen. Wait 20 seconds for your eyes to settle. Look for fixed bright areas that hug an edge or corner.

Move your head slightly left and right. IPS glow usually changes with your viewing angle. Backlight bleed tends to stay anchored to the same edge in the same shape.

Keep the camera honest

Phone cameras brighten dark scenes automatically. A long exposure can turn a mild glow into a white cloud. If you need a record, lower the phone exposure until the photo resembles what your eyes see.

Do not use the photo as the only verdict. Judge the panel during real content too. Watch a dark scene with subtitles or letterbox bars and note whether the bright area pulls your attention away from the picture.

Check for pressure

An overtight monitor arm, twisted chassis, or pressure from packaging can affect the edge. Make sure the display sits flat and no cable is pushing against the rear casing. Do not loosen panel screws unless the manufacturer tells you to.

When a return makes sense

Some edge glow is common on LCD panels. A return is reasonable when a patch is obvious at your normal brightness, in your normal room, from your normal seat. Save one honest photo, note the settings, and contact the seller while the return window is open.

OLED screens do not use an LCD backlight. Bright patches on an OLED need a different diagnosis, such as image retention, panel uniformity, or physical damage.

title: How to Test Screen Uniformity
description: Use gray and solid color fields to spot dirty screen effect, tint shifts, and uneven brightness across a display.
html:
Uniformity describes how evenly a screen shows the same tone from one edge to the other. Poor uniformity can look like cloudy patches, darker corners, colored bands, or a faint dirty layer during camera pans.

Start with middle gray

Open the grayscale test and choose a tone near 50 percent. View it fullscreen from your normal seat. Middle gray reveals brightness changes without the glare of a full white screen.

Let your eyes move across the panel instead of staring at one spot. Look for vertical bands, cloudy areas, and corners that fall darker than the center.

Check more than one level

Repeat the check at 5, 25, 50, 75, and 100 percent gray. A panel can look even at one level and uneven at another.

Use white to check edge brightness and color tint. Use dark gray to check near-black uniformity. On OLED, very dark gray may reveal vertical bands that are invisible during bright content.

Add solid colors

Run the color test and pause on red, green, and blue. A patch that looks neutral on gray but changes color on these fields may be a tint or subpixel issue rather than simple brightness variation.

Keep any color management mode consistent during the test. Switching picture presets halfway through makes comparison useless.

Try real movement

Uniformity problems often stand out when a flat scene moves. Use the motion test with a pale background and watch for stationary bands behind the moving object. Sports fields, skies, and slow game camera pans are common real-world checks.

Decide whether it matters

No large panel is perfectly uniform. The useful question is whether you notice the issue from your seat during content you actually use.

Document a problem with one gray photo and one real scene. Keep camera exposure close to what your eyes see. If a new display has a strong central band, obvious colored tint, or distracting dirty screen effect, contact the seller before the return window closes.

title: How to Test Motion Blur and Pixel Response
description: Check moving edges at several speeds and tell pixel response blur apart from refresh rate limits and overshoot.
html:
Motion blur on a display has more than one cause. The panel may change pixels slowly, the refresh rate may be low, or an aggressive overdrive setting may create a bright trail behind moving objects.

Match the display refresh rate

Open your system display settings and confirm the screen is using the refresh rate you paid for. A 144 Hz monitor running at 60 Hz will look worse before the test even begins.

Close video capture tools and heavy downloads. They can cause frame drops that look like a panel problem.

Run the moving target

Open the motion test in fullscreen. Start with a moderate speed. Track the object with your eyes, then look at a fixed point while it passes.

Increase the speed one step at a time. A soft trailing edge suggests slow pixel response. A bright or dark halo on the opposite edge often points to overdrive overshoot.

Compare overdrive settings

If the monitor has response time or overdrive controls, test each level at the same speed. Names like Fast and Extreme are marketing labels, not measurements.

The highest setting is often not the cleanest. Choose the level with the shortest trail and the least visible halo. Repeat at a lower refresh rate if you use variable refresh rate, since one overdrive mode may not suit the whole range.

Check dark transitions

VA panels can show extra smearing when dark shades move across a dark background. Test a dark target on middle gray, then a middle gray target on near black. Keep room lighting normal so your eyes do not overreact to tiny changes.

Know the limit of a browser test

A browser test is good for side-by-side settings and obvious artifacts. It does not replace a high-speed camera or instrumented response measurement. Browser timing, frame delivery, and the operating system can all affect the result.

Use the test to pick the cleanest setting for your own games and videos. If trails remain severe at the correct refresh rate and every overdrive level, save a short slow-motion phone video and contact the seller.
